open.speaker: fay
lines: You're the Americans. The ones at Mrs Bannister's. She said you'd come in, and she said you'd be polite about it, so I'll be polite back.
Before you ask me anything, I'm going to ask you something, and I'll know from the answer whether we're talking. What colour was the hat?
She's got her hands flat on the counter. That's a woman who's practised not moving.

passives.line: She has rehearsed this. Not the story, the asking. Every word of it has been said to a mirror, and the mirror never got it right either.
Stillness like that is older than she is. A child learns it in a room where something is listening. She has never unlearned it.

options.text: Yellow. Pointed. Taller than a man with it on. But that's not the part you care about.
(Say nothing. Let her see you're not going to guess.)
We read the paper, Miss Mallory. We're not here to be graded.
You tell me. You're the one who was there.

test_pass.speaker: fay
lines: ...No. It isn't. Everybody knows yellow. Colin told everybody yellow, and yellow was the bit they could laugh at, so yellow's the bit that stuck.
All right. Sit down, there's a chair. I'll say it once and I'll say it properly, and then you'll be the third.

test_silent.speaker: fay
lines: Good. It was yellow. Nobody has ever asked me what the rest of it was, and I think that's because nobody wanted to know.
Sit down. I'll say it once.

test_other.speaker: fay
lines: No. You don't get to be clever about it. I was seven and I have had twenty-one years of clever, and clever is what my father was at breakfast when Colin cried.
...Yellow. It was yellow. I'll tell you once, because Mr Harwood's gone to the bank and he'd want me to. Then that's it.

story.speaker: fay
lines: Tuesday. Hot. We were down by the brook catching sticklebacks in a jar and it was standing in the reeds, and it was all colours. Not striped, not spotted. The colour of it went across it like weather goes across a field. It never stayed.

The hat was the only thing that stayed. Yellow, pointed, higher than a man. And it bent down and it said, come and see the dials, and we went, because we were seven, and it was a hut, and the hut was full of dials. Walls of them. And the sea behind, through a window, which it couldn't be.
I drew it that week. On the back of a hymn sheet first, then properly, with the dials. I put numbers on them. I thought if I put numbers on them it would be true.
Numbers on the dials. She was seven. You put numbers on things when you want to be believed.

passives.line: Numbers on the dials, added afterward. A child remembers colours; the numbers are what an adult goes back for. She has looked at that drawing a great deal since 1973, and it is upstairs, and she has not offered it.

hub.speaker: fay
lines: That's what happened. Ask what you like. I'll answer what I can and I'll tell you when I can't.

static.line: It's upstairs. You can hear it through the ceiling, the paper, the way paper sounds when it's been folded for twenty years. Ask for it. Ask now, while Harwood's out.

options.text: You've told this to a mirror more than you've told it to people.
The paper said a stray dog and the heat. A dog doesn't need a hut full of dials.
Show us the drawing, Fay. Not for the file. For you.
That's all for now. Thank you.

mirror.speaker: fay
lines: ...Every night for a year. Then every birthday. Then just the 29th of May, in the afternoon, on the Levels, out loud, to the reeds. Mr Harwood gives me the afternoon. He thinks I don't know he knows.
You're the first person who's noticed I was rehearsed and not minded. Most people think rehearsed means made up. It means the opposite. You don't rehearse a lie, it comes out fine on its own.
You were kind. She noticed that too.

mirror_fail.speaker: fay
lines: I've told it to nobody. That's what nobody means. ...A mirror. Is that what you lot do, in America, with the lights and the sofa?
Ask me something about the hut. That I can answer.

paper.speaker: fay
lines: Dr Gale wrote 'sunstroke' and the sergeant wrote 'Alsatian' and the paper wrote both, and my father bought them each a drink. Everybody bought everybody a drink that week. It was that kind of story.

I had sunstroke. I'm not saying I didn't; I was sick for two days and I saw patterns on the ceiling. But I was sick on the Wednesday. I saw it on the Tuesday. Nobody at the Mermaid was interested in which day.
Tuesday, then Wednesday. That's a sequence, not a symptom. Fine. Noted.

paper_fail.speaker: fay
lines: You read it, then. Good. Then you know what the island decided, and you can decide the same, and save yourselves the ferry.
I'm sorry. That's not fair to you. It's just that the paper's the one thing everybody read.

drawing.speaker: fay
lines: ...Mind the shop. If anyone comes in for a prescription, tell them ten minutes. If anyone comes in for anything else, they can wait.

Here. Don't touch the crayon, it comes off. Blue, red, green, yellow. Left to right. He turned them in that order and the wall opened, and that's the part I didn't make up, and that's the part nobody ever asked about.
The numbers are mine. I was seven. Take a picture of it if you want. I'd rather keep the paper, if that's all right. It's been upstairs twenty-one years and I think it would miss the ceiling.
Blue, red, green, yellow. If there's a wall of dials anywhere on this island, that's the combination, and she's had it in a drawer since she was seven.
Thank you, dear. Nobody's going to laugh in this shop. I'll see to it.

drawing_fail.speaker: fay
lines: 'For you.' I've kept it twenty-one years from people who were kinder than you and worse at it. You can put down that I said no, and you can put down why, and the why is that you said 'for you' like you'd read it off a card.
There's a bell on the door. Mr Harwood will be back at two.

passives.line: That was Rapport talking, not you, and it was reading off a card. She heard the card. You hear the bell, and you did not touch the door.
